claim: Membralin mutant mice manifest a severe and early-onset motor neuron disease in an autosomal recessive manner, dying by postnatal day 5–6.
source: Membralin mutant mice manifest a severe and early-onset motor neuron disease in an autosomal recessive manner, dying by postnatal day 5–6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of the phenotype of membralin mutant mice described in the manuscript.

claim: Selective death of lower motor neurons, including those innervating the limbs, intercostal muscles, and diaphragm, is predominantly responsible for the fatal phenotype in membralin mutant mice.
source: Selective death of lower motor neurons, including those innervating the limbs, intercostal muscles, and diaphragm, is predominantly responsible for this fatal phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and electron microscopy data showing selective motor neuron loss in the manuscript.

claim: Neural expression of a membralin transgene completely rescues membralin mutant mice.
source: Neural expression of a membralin transgene completely rescues membralin mutant mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that transgenic expression of membralin rescues the DKO phenotype.

claim: Membralin interacts with Erlin2, an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein that is located in lipid rafts and known to be important in ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
source: Mechanistically, we show that membralin interacts with Erlin2, an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein that is located in lipid rafts and known to be important in ER-associated protein degradation (ERAD).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET and co-immunoprecipitation experiments, as well as citation to prior knowledge about Erlin2.

claim: The degradation rate of ERAD substrates is attenuated in cells lacking membralin.
source: Accordingly, the degradation rate of ERAD substrates is attenuated in cells lacking membralin.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase experiments showing slower degradation of CD3-δ in membralin KO MEFs.

claim: Membralin mutations or deficiency in mouse models induces ER stress, rendering neurons more vulnerable to cell death.
source: Membralin mutations or deficiency in mouse models induces ER stress, rendering neurons more vulnerable to cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased ER stress markers and cell viability assays showing increased vulnerability to ER stress inducers.

claim: Increased ER stress is thought to play an early role in motor neuron diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT).
source: Increased ER stress is thought to play an early role in motor neuron diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) (Atkin et al., 2006; Nagata et al., 2007; Nishitoh et al., 2008; Kanekura et al., 2009; Saxena et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ER stress in motor neuron diseases.

claim: Many ER stress-related molecules are upregulated in SOD1 mice at an early stage of the disease, and some are specific to motor neurons.
source: Many ER stress-related molecules are upregulated in SOD1 mice at an early stage of the disease, and some are specific to motor neurons (Tobisawa et al., 2003; Atkin et al., 2006; Kikuchi et al., 2006; Nagata et al., 2007; Ito et al., 2009; Saxena et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on SOD1 mouse models.

claim: Genetic interruption of UPR signaling molecules, such as XBP-1 or apoptosis signal-regulating kinase1 (ASK1), protects motor neurons in SOD1 mutant mice.
source: Moreover, genetic interruption of UPR signaling molecules, such as XBP-1 or apoptosis signal-regulating kinase1 (ASK1), protects motor neurons in SOD1 mutant mice (Nishitoh et al., 2008; Hetz and Mollereau, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on genetic manipulation of UPR signaling in SOD1 mice.

claim: ER stress inhibitors, such as salubrinal, guanabenz, and sphin1, delay disease onset and prolong the survival of SOD1 mutant mice.
source: Importantly, ER stress inhibitors, such as salubrinal, guanabenz, and sphin1, delay disease onset and prolong the survival of these mutant mice (Saxena et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014; Das et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on pharmacological inhibition of ER stress in SOD1 mice.

claim: Membralin had been predicted by genome sequencing to encompass an open reading frame (orf61 in mouse and c19orf6 in human), but the function of the encoded protein has remained unknown.
source: Previously, membralin had been predicted by genome sequencing to encompass an open reading frame (orf61 in mouse and c19orf6 in human), but the function of the encoded protein has, heretofore, remained unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on prior genomic sequencing data and the absence of functional characterization in the literature.

claim: Orf61 is highly conserved and found in the genome of most species except yeast and bacteria.
source: Orf61 is highly conserved and found in the genome of most species except yeast and bacteria.
evidence: This claim is based on comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The protein encoded by orf61 was named membralin because it was predicted to be a membrane protein.
source: cDNAs for membralin have been cloned from human and mouse tissues (Andersson and von Euler, 2002; Chen et al., 2005), and the protein encoded by orf61 was named membralin because it was predicted to be a membrane protein (Andersson and von Euler, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on membralin cloning and nomenclature.

claim: The 3′ end of the GluN3B gene overlaps with the 3′ end of the membralin gene on the opposite strand.
source: Here, we discovered during our cloning and characterization of the glutamate receptor subunit 3B gene (GluN3B, formerly designated NR3B, Nishi et al., 2001; Chatterton et al., 2002; Matsuda et al., 2002) that the 3′ end of the GluN3B gene overlaps with the 3′ end of the membralin gene on the opposite strand.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analysis and sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GluN3B/membralin C-terminal double-knockout (DKO) mice die at postnatal day 5–6 of paresis due to severe motor neuron degeneration.
source: We observed that GluN3B/membralin C-terminal double-knockout (DKO) mice die at postnatal day 5–6 of paresis due to severe motor neuron degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of the DKO mouse phenotype.

claim: Transgenic expression of membralin, but not GluN3B, rescued the phenotypes of DKO mice.
source: Transgenic expression of membralin, but not GluN3B, rescued the phenotypes of DKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential rescue effects of membralin and GluN3B transgenes.

claim: Membralin-specific KO mice phenocopied the DKO mice.
source: Additionally, we generated membralin-specific KO mice and found that they phenocopied the DKO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar phenotypes in membralin-specific KO and DKO mice.

claim: Neurons from membralin mutant mice display increased basal ER stress and increased vulnerability to ER stress-inducing agents.
source: Additionally, neurons from membralin mutant mice display increased basal ER stress and increased vulnerability to ER stress-inducing agents.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data and cell viability assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: DKO mice appeared normal at birth but unexpectedly died at postnatal day 5–6 (P5-6).
source: DKO mice appeared normal at birth but unexpectedly died at postnatal day 5–6 (P5-6).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data on DKO mouse survival.

claim: The motor function of DKO mice was indistinguishable from WT or heterozygous littermates during the first three postnatal days, but motor strength was severely impaired thereafter, preceding death.
source: The motor function of these mice was indistinguishable from WT or heterozygous littermates during the first three postnatal days, but motor strength was severely impaired, thereafter, preceding death.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral observations of DKO mice.

claim: DKO mice were significantly smaller than WT and heterozygous littermates.
source: DKO mice were also significantly smaller than WT and heterozygous littermates (Figure 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by visual and quantitative comparison of mouse size shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DKO mice displayed normal gross anatomy and histology in the brain, visceral organs, and skeletal muscle.
source: but displayed normal gross anatomy and histology in the brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), visceral organs, and skeletal muscle.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological examination shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of motor neurons in DKO mice was unchanged at P0 and P3, but reduced by 40% at P5, compared to littermate WT controls.
source: The number of motor neurons in DKO mice was unchanged at P0 and P3, but reduced by 40% at P5, compared to littermate WT controls (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of motor neuron numbers shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The remaining motor neurons in DKO mice at P5 appeared smaller than those of WT mice.
source: The remaining motor neurons appeared smaller than those of WT mice.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological observations of motor neurons.

claim: Motor neuron loss and surrounding astrogliosis were apparent in the cervical spinal cords of P5 DKO mice.
source: Motor neuron loss and surrounding astrogliosis were also apparent in the cervical spinal cords of P5 DKO mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: By P3, DKO mice had increased Isg15 expression in the ventral horn of the cervical and lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord.
source: In contrast, by P3, DKO mice had increased Isg15 expression in the ventral horn of the cervical and lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: By P5, DKO mice showed increased Isg15 expression in additional areas containing primary motor neurons, with highest expression in the ventral horn of all segments of the spinal cord and moderate expression in the facial nucleus of the brainstem.
source: By P5, DKO mice showed increased Isg15 expression in additional areas containing primary motor neurons, with highest expression in the ventral horn of all segments of the spinal cord and moderate expression in the facial nucleus of the brainstem (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: No Isg15 expression was detectable in other brain areas of DKO mice, even in late-stage mice.
source: No Isg15 expression was detectable in other brain areas, even in late-stage DKO mice.
evidence: This claim is based on immunostaining observations.

claim: The normal process of programmed cell death in embryonic motor neurons is complete at birth.
source: Since the normal process of programmed cell death in embryonic motor neurons is complete at birth (Lance-Jones, 1982)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on developmental motor neuron death.

claim: The loss of motor neurons in DKO mice was most likely due to cellular events occurring perinatally.
source: the loss of motor neurons in DKO mice was most likely due to cellular events occurring perinatally.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing of motor neuron loss and the completion of developmental programmed cell death at birth.

claim: Motor neuron axons in the ventral root of DKO mice showed advanced degeneration.
source: Motor neuron axons in the ventral root of DKO mice showed advanced degeneration (Figure 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Sensory neuron axons in the dorsal root of DKO mice were intact.
source: whereas sensory neuron axons in the dorsal root were intact (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Motor neuron axons in DKO mice showed intra-axonal vacuoles and the loss of axoplasm, as well as disintegrated myelin and amorphous lipids, as typically seen in Wallerian degeneration.
source: Under high magnification of motor neuron axons, we saw intra-axonal vacuoles and the loss of axoplasm (Figure 1G), as well as disintegrated myelin and amorphous lipids (Figure 1H), as typically seen in Wallerian degeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1G,H and comparison to known features of Wallerian degeneration.

claim: The percentage of degenerated axons in the ventral root of DKO mice reached 48.0 ± 4.1% by P5, which was significantly greater (p < 0.01) than in WT mice (8.6 ± 1.5%).
source: The percentage of degenerated axons in the ventral root of DKO mice reached 48.0 ± 4.1% by P5, which was significantly greater (p < 0.01) than in WT mice (8.6 ± 1.5%) (Figure 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axonal degeneration shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The percentage of degenerated axons in the dorsal root of DKO mice (10.5 ± 1.9%) was similar to that of the WT ventral root, consistent with the normal background level of axonal degeneration that occurs during development.
source: In contrast, the percentage of degenerated axons in the dorsal root of DKO mice (10.5 ± 1.9%) was similar to that of the WT ventral root, consistent with the normal background level of axonal degeneration that occurs during development.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis and comparison to normal developmental processes.

claim: The sensory afferent terminals in the spinal cord of DKO mice appeared normal.
source: Moreover, the sensory afferent terminals in the spinal cord of DKO mice appeared normal (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Degeneration of phrenic motor nerve fibers and terminals was found in P5 DKO mice.
source: In contrast, we found degeneration of phrenic motor nerve fibers and terminals in P5 DKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: The selective death of motor neurons in DKO mice potentially leads to respiratory failure due to loss of motor neuron innervation of the intercostal muscles and diaphragm.
source: These results further confirm the selective death of motor neurons in DKO mice, potentially leading to respiratory failure due to loss of motor neuron innervation of the intercostal muscles and diaphragm.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed degeneration of phrenic motor neurons and the known role of these neurons in respiration.

claim: DKO mice present a phenotype of early-onset and apparently selective motor neuron degeneration.
source: Taken together, our DKO mice present a phenotype of early-onset and apparently selective motor neuron degeneration.
evidence: This claim summarizes the experimental findings on DKO mouse phenotype.

claim: Tg (membralin) mice were fertile, normal in size, and did not display any gross physical or behavioral abnormalities compared with their littermate controls.
source: The membralin transgenic mice [Tg (membralin)] were fertile, normal in size, and did not display any gross physical or behavioral abnormalities compared with their littermate controls.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data on Tg (membralin) mice.

claim: When Tg (membralin) mice were crossbred with DKO mice, the DKO/Tg (membralin) mice were apparently normal, manifesting neither paresis nor premature death.
source: When Tg (membralin) mice were crossbred with DKO mice, the DKO/Tg (membralin) mice were apparently normal, manifesting neither paresis nor premature death (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data and survival curves shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The membralin transgene rescued DKO mice, even though membralin mRNA levels remained somewhat lower than in WT mice.
source: Thus, the membralin transgene rescued DKO mice, even though membralin mRNA levels remained somewhat lower than in WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C and survival data.

claim: Membralin/GFP transgene expression was predominantly neuronal, although relatively weak expression in glial cells could not be ruled out.
source: GFP immunostaining in the ventral horn of the spinal cord showed that membralin/GFP transgene expression was predominantly neuronal, although we could not rule out relatively weak expression in glial cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The DKO/Tg (membralin) mice showed no sign of motor defects or motor neuron loss, despite the absence of GluN3B expression.
source: The DKO/Tg (membralin) mice showed no sign of motor defects or motor neuron loss, despite the absence of GluN3B expression (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational and histological data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The GluN3B transgene did not rescue DKO mice.
source: In contrast, the GluN3B transgene did not rescue DKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: GluN3B KO mice generated by deleting the first exon did not show any defect in motor neurons.
source: and GluN3B KO mice generated by deleting the first exon did not show any defect in motor neurons (Niemann et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on GluN3B KO mice.

claim: The loss of intact membralin in DKO mice causes motor neuron degeneration.
source: Taken together, these findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the loss of intact membralin in DKO mice causes motor neuron degeneration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiments and the phenotype of membralin-specific KO mice.

claim: Heterozygous DKO mice did not manifest motor defects.
source: Since heterozygous DKO mice did not manifest motor defects
evidence: This claim is based on observational data on heterozygous DKO mice.

claim: Expression of the truncated form of membralin appears to lack any deleterious effect.
source: and expression of the truncated form of membralin appears to lack any deleterious effect.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the normal phenotype of heterozygous DKO mice.

claim: Homozygous mice carrying membralin/trapping vector alleles did not express membralin mRNAs with sequences beyond exon 2.
source: RT-PCR experiments using primers from exon 1 and 2 further confirmed that homozygous mice carrying membralin/trapping vector alleles did not express membralin mRNAs with sequences beyond exon 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data on gene-trapped membralin KO mice.

claim: Membralin protein was reduced in heterozygotes and absent in homozygotes of the gene-trapped KO line.
source: Membralin protein was also reduced in heterozygotes and absent in homozygotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data on gene-trapped membralin KO mice.

claim: Membralin KO mice (gene-trapped line) phenocopied the DKO mice in motor defects, with ∼50% motor neuron loss preceding death around P5.
source: These membralin KO mice phenocopied the DKO mice in motor defects, with ∼50% motor neuron loss preceding death around P5 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational and histological data shown in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Membralin mRNA was expressed in multiple tissues, including brain and spinal cord, but not heart, skeletal muscle, or spleen.
source: RT-PCR analysis showed that membralin mRNA was expressed in multiple tissues, including brain and spinal cord, but not heart, skeletal muscle, or spleen (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Western blot analysis of spinal cord samples from WT and KO mice showed specific expression of membralin in the ER but not in the cytosol or mitochondria.
source: Western blot analysis of spinal cord samples from WT and KO mice showed specific expression of membralin in the ER but not in the cytosol or mitochondria (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data on subcellular fractions shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Membralin-myc co-localized with an ER marker PDI but not with markers for Golgi or mitochondria.
source: Immunocytochemistry demonstrated that membralin-myc co-localized with an ER marker PDI but not with markers for Golgi or mitochondria (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Membralin-myc was not expressed on the cell surface.
source: Membralin-myc was not expressed on the cell surface, since it was not detected in transfected cells without first permeabilizing the membrane (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on immunocytochemistry experiments with and without membrane permeabilization.

claim: Membralin is most likely a transmembrane protein with 4–6 membrane-spanning regions, containing an ER-lumen domain between membrane-spanning regions 1 and 2.
source: Software for topology prediction from the Center for Biological Sequences (CBS, TMHMM) indicated that the membralin is most likely a transmembrane protein with 4–6 membrane-spanning regions, containing an ER-lumen domain between membrane-spanning regions 1 and 2.
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of protein topology.

claim: Membralin has multiple glycosylation sites and cytosolic regions at both the N-terminal ends and C-terminal ends.
source: Additionally, the protein has multiple glycosylation sites and cytosolic regions at both the N-terminal ends and C-terminal ends (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Membralin is a membrane protein most likely localized to the ER and/or outer nuclear envelope.
source: These data suggest that membralin is a membrane protein most likely localized to the ER and/or outer nuclear envelope.
evidence: This claim is inferred from subcellular localization and topology prediction data.

claim: A recent study identified a potential interaction of membralin (C19orf6) with Erlin2 through an integrative mapping strategy of human ERAD networks.
source: A recent study defining human ERAD networks through an integrative mapping strategy identified a potential interaction of membralin (C19orf6) with Erlin2 (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on ERAD networks.

claim: Erlin2 is a protein that is enriched in ER lipid rafts.
source: Erlin2 is a protein that is enriched in ER lipid rafts (Ikegawa et al., 1999; Browman et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on Erlin2 localization.

claim: Mutations in Erlin2 have been linked to several human diseases with motor dysfunction.
source: and mutations in Erlin2 have been linked to several human diseases with motor dysfunction (Al-Yahyaee et al., 2006; Alazami et al., 2011; Yildirim et al., 2011; Al-Saif et al., 2012; Wakil et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on Erlin2 mutations and disease.

claim: GFP-tagged membralin not only co-localized with but also manifested a strong FRET signal with mCherry-tagged Erlin2 in the ER.
source: We found that GFP-tagged membralin not only co-localized with but also manifested a strong FRET signal with mCherry-tagged Erlin2 in the ER (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The FRET efficiency was significantly higher for GFP-tagged membralin and mCherry-tagged Erlin2 (18.00 ± 0.70%) than the negative control (GFP and mCherry, 0.15 ± 0.05%), consistent with a direct interaction of the two molecules.
source: The FRET efficiency was significantly higher for GFP-tagged membralin and mCherry-tagged Erlin2 (18.00 ± 0.70%) than the negative control (GFP and mCherry, 0.15 ± 0.05%), consistent with a direct interaction of the two molecules (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative FRET efficiency data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Myc-tagged full-length membralin co-immunoprecipitated with HA-tagged Erlin2.
source: Additionally, Myc-tagged full-length membralin co-immunoprecipitated with HA-tagged Erlin2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The interaction of membralin with Erlin2 supports the notion that membralin is an ER membrane protein.
source: This interaction of membralin with Erlin2 further supports the notion that membralin is an ER membrane protein
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known localization of Erlin2 and the demonstrated interaction with membralin.

claim: Loss of membralin could potentially increase ER stress by interrupting ERAD.
source: and also suggests that loss of membralin could potentially increase ER stress by interrupting ERAD.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the interaction with Erlin2 and its role in ERAD.

claim: The ER membrane protein, CD3-δ, was cleared more slowly in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) prepared from membralin KO mice than from WT mice.
source: Indeed, we found that the ER membrane protein, CD3-δ, was cleared more slowly in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) prepared from membralin KO mice than from WT mice (Figure 5D)
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase degradation assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There was no change in the clearance of the ER lumenal protein, NHK, in membralin KO MEFs compared to WT MEFs.
source: whereas there was no change in the clearance of the ER lumenal protein, NHK (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase degradation assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Membralin deficiency affects degradation of ER membrane proteins, which could potentially increase ER stress.
source: These results suggest that membralin deficiency affects degradation of ER membrane proteins, which could potentially increase ER stress.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects on degradation of ER membrane vs. lumenal proteins.

claim: The levels of GRP78 and ATF4 were consistently higher in the spinal cord of P3 membralin KO mice than WT mice (154 ± 35% and 412 ± 39% of WT, respectively).
source: Western blot analysis showed that the levels of GRP78 and ATF4, two molecules induced during ER stress via activation of the PERK signaling pathway, were consistently higher in the spinal cord of P3 membralin KO mice than WT mice (154 ± 35% and 412 ± 39% of WT, respectively; KO, n = 4; WT, n = 3; Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot quantification data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Levels of spliced XBP-1, indicating activation of the IRE1 signaling pathway during ER stress, were not altered in membralin KO mice.
source: In contrast, levels of spliced XBP-1, indicating activation of the IRE1 signaling pathway during ER stress, were not altered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tunicamycin produced a greater degree of cell death in MEFs from KO mice than from WT mice.
source: Furthermore, tunicamycin, an inducer of ER stress, produced a greater degree of cell death in MEFs from KO mice than from WT mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tunicamycin exposure increased CHOP and ATF4 levels earlier and to a greater extent in MEFs from KO mice; GRP78 levels were also higher at 24 hr post-exposure.
source: Tunicamycin exposure also increased CHOP and ATF4 levels earlier and to a greater extent in MEFs from KO mice; GRP78 levels were also higher at 24 hr post-exposure (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot time course data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Basal levels of ATF4, but not CHOP, were higher in membralin KO mice than WT mice.
source: Basal levels of ATF4, but not CHOP, were higher in membralin KO mice than WT mice (Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data at baseline shown in Figure 6C.

claim: XBP-1 splicing was not altered in membralin KO MEFs.
source: but XBP-1 splicing was not altered (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loss of membralin increases basal ER stress and makes cells more vulnerable to additional ER stress-induced injury.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that loss of membralin increases basal ER stress and makes cells more vulnerable to additional ER stress-induced injury.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on ER stress markers and cell viability.

claim: Hereditary motor neuropathy (HMN) is usually subdivided into two groups: proximal HMN (classical spinal muscular atrophy syndromes) and distal HMN (which clinically resemble CMT syndromes without obvious sensory abnormalities).
source: Hereditary motor neuropathy (HMN) is usually subdivided into two groups: proximal HMN, i.e., classical spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) syndromes, and distal HMN, which clinically resemble CMT syndromes without obvious sensory abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is based on established clinical classification of motor neuropathies.

claim: Distal HMN represents a heterogeneous group of peripheral neuropathies affecting mainly distal muscles with both autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance.
source: In contrast to proximal HMN, distal HMN represents a heterogeneous group of peripheral neuropathies affecting mainly distal muscles with both autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance (Irobi et al., 2004, 2006; Irobi-Devolder, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior reviews on distal HMN.

claim: A dozen causal gene loci and other associated genes have been identified for distal HMN (exclusive of type I).
source: A dozen of causal gene loci and other associated genes have been identified for distal HMN (exclusive of type I); these genes encode for a functionally heterogeneous group of proteins, as summarized in recent reviews (Irobi et al., 2004, 2006; Irobi-Devolder, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior reviews on distal HMN genetics.

claim: The biological functions of proteins affected in distal HMN include stress responses (small heat shock proteins HSP22, HSP27), housekeeping (GARS, glycyl tRNA synthetase), protein glycosylation in the ER (seipin), RNA processing (immunoglobulin μ-binding protein 2 [LGHMBP2] and senataxin), and axonal transport (dynactin).
source: The biological functions of the affected proteins include stress responses (small heat shock proteins HSP22, HSP27), housekeeping (GARS, glycyl tRNA synthetase), protein glycosylation in the ER (seipin), RNA processing (immunoglobulin μ-binding protein 2 [LGHMBP2] and senataxin), and axonal transport (dynactin).
evidence: This claim is based on known functions of genes associated with distal HMN.

claim: It is not clear how mutated proteins of diverse cellular function converge to affect motor neuron survival selectively in distal HMN.
source: It is not clear, however, how these mutated proteins of diverse cellular function converge to affect motor neuron survival selectively.
evidence: This claim reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The expression of proteins affected in distal HMN is not restricted to motor neurons.
source: In fact, their expression is not even restricted to motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on known expression patterns of genes associated with distal HMN.

claim: Motor neurons may have an unusual susceptibility to various forms of cell stress, particularly ER stress.
source: A hint towards pathogenesis may be found in prior work in conjunction with our new findings and involves an unusual susceptibility of motor neurons to various forms of cell stress, particularly ER stress.
evidence: This claim is speculated based on prior work and the findings in this study.

claim: The membralin KO mouse provides a good model to study selective motor neuron vulnerability.
source: Accordingly, the membralin KO mouse generated in our laboratory provides a good model to study selective motor neuron vulnerability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotype of membralin KO mice.

claim: Membralin KO mice display severe motor neuron loss and muscle wasting, leading to paresis and death.
source: These mice display severe motor neuron loss and muscle wasting, leading to paresis and death.
evidence: This claim summarizes the phenotype of membralin KO mice.

claim: The early disease onset in membralin KO mice is similar to that seen in an SMA mouse model.
source: Although the early disease onset in membralin KO mice is similar to that seen in an SMA mouse model (Hsieh-Li et al., 2000; Monani et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is based on comparison to prior SMA mouse models cited in the text.

claim: The pattern of motor neuron injury in membralin KO mice is reminiscent of human distal HMN rather than proximal HMN, as observed in SMA.
source: the pattern of motor neuron injury in membralin KO mice is reminiscent of human distal HMN rather than proximal HMN, as observed in SMA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the pattern of motor neuron loss observed in membralin KO mice.

claim: Of the dozen known causal genes for distal HMN, only a few show autosomal recessive inheritance, and no mouse model has been generated.
source: Of the dozen known causal genes for distal HMN, only a few show autosomal recessive inheritance, and no mouse model has, heretofore, been generated (Irobi et al., 2004, 2006; Irobi-Devolder, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior reviews on distal HMN.

claim: The membralin null mouse represents a novel model for human distal HMN.
source: Therefore, the membralin null mouse represents a novel model for human distal HMN.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotype of membralin KO mice and the lack of prior models.

claim: Membralin is mainly located in the ER based on endogenous and heterologous expression studies.
source: Additionally, our studies demonstrate the previously unknown function of membralin in motor neuron survival. Our findings from endogenous and heterologous expression studies suggest that membralin is mainly located in the ER.
evidence: This claim is supported by subcellular fractionation and immunocytochemistry data.

claim: Relatively low expression of membralin seems sufficient for normal function, as heterozygotes of the membralin KO survived, and transgene rescue of the membralin KO did not require high expression levels.
source: Relatively low expression of membralin seems sufficient for normal function, as heterozygotes of the membralin KO survived, and transgene rescue of the membralin KO did not require high expression levels.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival of heterozygotes and the rescue with low transgene expression.

claim: In rescue experiments, membralin transgene expression was primarily in brain, not muscle, consistent with the notion that the pathogenic process is predominantly neural in origin.
source: Importantly, in our rescue experiments, membralin transgene expression was primarily in brain, not muscle, consistent with the notion that the pathogenic process is predominantly neural in origin.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data showing tissue-specific transgene expression.

claim: The exact mechanisms underlying motor neuron death in membralin KO mice are not yet clear.
source: The exact mechanisms underlying motor neuron death in membralin KO mice are not yet clear
evidence: This claim acknowledges the limitations of current understanding.

claim: Motor neuron death in membralin KO mice occurs very rapidly at an early and well-defined postnatal stage.
source: although death occurs very rapidly at an early and well-defined postnatal stage.
evidence: This claim is based on observational data on the timing of motor neuron death.

claim: Membralin KO mice can be used as an early-onset model of motor neuron disease.
source: Thus, membralin KO mice can be used not only as an early-onset model of motor neuron disease
evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotype and timing of disease in membralin KO mice.

claim: Membralin KO mice can be used to determine if there are features in common with late-onset motor neuron disease, such as motor neuron-specific vulnerability to ER stress, dying back axonopathy, or non-cell autonomous death.
source: but also to determine if there are features in common with late-onset motor neuron disease, such as motor neuron-specific vulnerability to ER stress (Saxena et al., 2009; Roselli and Caroni, 2015), dying back axonopathy (Fischer et al., 2004; Coleman, 2005), or non-cell autonomous death (Boillee et al., 2006; Yamanaka et al., 2008; Kang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is speculated based on potential applications of the model and citations to prior research on motor neuron disease mechanisms.

claim: Membralin was predicted to encode a transmembrane protein, but it lacked homology with any known protein domains and was not known to interact with other membrane proteins.
source: Previously, membralin was predicted to encode a transmembrane protein, but it lacked homology with any known protein domains and was not known to interact with other membrane proteins (Andersson and von Euler, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on membralin.

claim: The exact cellular functions of Erlin2 are not clear.
source: The exact cellular functions of Erlin2 are not clear
evidence: This claim reflects the current state of knowledge about Erlin2.

claim: Erlin2 has been reported to interact with several ER resident E3 ligases such as GP78 and Hrd1 that are important for ERAD.
source: although it has been reported to interact with several ER resident E3 ligases such as GP78 and Hrd1 that are important for ERAD (Christianson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on Erlin2 interactions.

claim: Erlin2 has been shown to regulate ER membrane proteins such as Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors.
source: Additionally, Erlin2 has been shown to regulate ER membrane proteins such as Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors (Pearce et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on Erlin2 function.

claim: It is conceivable that membralin assists Erlin2 in a complex that retrotranslocates unfolded proteins from the ER lumen to the cytosol, thus facilitating their ubiquitination for degradation.
source: It is conceivable that membralin assists Erlin2 in a complex that retrotranslocates unfolded proteins from the ER lumen to the cytosol, thus facilitating their ubiquitination for degradation (Schulze et al., 2005; Carvalho et al., 2006; Denic et al., 2006; Vembar and Brodsky, 2008; Carvalho et al., 2010; Smith et al., 2011; Brodsky, 2012).
evidence: This claim is speculated based on the interaction with Erlin2 and citations to prior research on ERAD mechanisms.

claim: Membralin deficiency might increase both basal ER stress and vulnerability to ER stress-induced cell death.
source: Consequently, membralin deficiency might increase both basal ER stress and vulnerability to ER stress-induced cell death, and this is exactly what we observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on ER stress markers and cell viability.

claim: ISGylation represents a type I interferon-dependent, ER stress-triggered event.
source: We also found differences in Isg15 levels in membralin KO mice, leading to ISGylation, a process that represents a type I interferon-dependent, ER stress-triggered event.
evidence: This claim is based on known functions of ISG15 and ISGylation.

claim: ISGylation is a pre-symptomatic event observed in a mouse model of ALS.
source: This observation is interesting in light of prior findings showing that ISGylation is a pre-symptomatic event observed in a mouse model of ALS (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on ISGylation in ALS models.

claim: The loss of membralin may contribute to degeneration by increasing ER stress in motor neurons, which are especially vulnerable to such stress due to their large metabolic demand.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that the loss of membralin may contribute to degeneration by increasing ER stress in motor neurons, which are especially vulnerable to such stress due to their large metabolic demand.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and known properties of motor neurons.

claim: The metabolic demand of motor neurons is particularly prevalent postnatally when maturation of motor neurons requires synthesis of proteins for production of dendritic trees, synaptic connections, and ionic conductances.
source: This demand is particularly prevalent postnatally when maturation of motor neurons requires synthesis of proteins for production of dendritic trees, synaptic connections, and ionic conductances (Vinay et al., 2000; Carrascal et al., 2005; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on motor neuron development.

claim: Disruption of ERAD in SOD1 mutant mice is known to induce ER stress, activation of ASK1, and motor neuron cell death.
source: Additionally, disruption of ERAD in SOD1 mutant mice is known to induce ER stress, activation of ASK1, and motor neuron cell death (Nishitoh et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research on ERAD disruption in SOD1 mice.

claim: Mutations in Erlin2 have been linked to intellectual disability, motor dysfunction, hereditary spastic paraplegia, and juvenile primary lateral sclerosis.
source: Mutations in Erlin2 have been linked to human disease, including intellectual disability, motor dysfunction, hereditary spastic paraplegia, and juvenile primary lateral sclerosis (Al-Saif et al., 2012; Al-Yahyaee et al., 2006; Alazami et al., 2011; Wakil et al., 2013; Yildirim et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on Erlin2 mutations and disease.

claim: Disturbance in various components of ERAD, including OS-9, erasin, ubiquilin2, torsinA, and Derlin1, causes ER stress.
source: Moreover, disturbance in various other components of ERAD, including OS-9, erasin, ubiquilin2, torsinA, and Derlin1, causes ER stress (Nishitoh et al., 2008; Alcock and Swanton, 2009; Lim et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2011; Nery et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on ERAD components and ER stress.

claim: Some ERAD component genes have been linked to ALS.
source: and some of these genes have been linked to ALS (Nishitoh et al., 2008; Alcock and Swanton, 2009; Lim et al., 2009; Alazami et al., 2011; Nery et al., 2011; Yildirim et al., 2011; Al-Saif et al., 2012; Wakil et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research linking ERAD genes to ALS.

claim: Future elucidation of the exact role of membralin in ERAD will be important for understanding the contribution of ER stress to motor neuron diseases.
source: Therefore, future elucidation of the exact role of membralin in ERAD will undoubtedly be important for understanding the contribution of ER stress to motor neuron diseases.
evidence: This claim is speculated about future research directions.

claim: There are more than 50 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the coding region of human membralin that result in missense mutations.
source: Interestingly, there are more than 50 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the coding region of human membralin that result in missense mutations (NBCI SNP database).
evidence: This claim is based on data from the NCBI SNP database.

claim: The minor allele frequency of most SNPs in human membralin is either low or has not been determined, suggesting that these SNPs are not common in the human population.
source: The minor allele frequency of most SNPs is either low or has not been determined, suggesting that these SNPs are not common in the human population.
evidence: This claim is inferred from SNP database information.

claim: The studies point to a specific role of membralin in motor neuron survival and potentially open a new avenue for research in the field of human motor neuron diseases.
source: Thus, our studies point to a specific role of membralin in motor neuron survival and potentially open a new avenue for research in the field of human motor neuron diseases.
evidence: This claim summarizes the implications of the study.
